knowledge:
- key_parameters: image.files=Path to folder containing images or vector of image file paths ;; nframes=Number of frames to load into the Frames object ;; mode=Color channel to extract (e.g., "red", "green") ;; brush.size=Size of the brush for morphological operations in preprocessing ;; L=Maximum displacement in pixels expected for a particle between consecutive frames ;; R=Link range, i.e., the number of future frames to consider for linking (typically 1 to 3) ;; acquisitionFrequency=Time interval between frames in milliseconds ;; scala=Spatial scale conversion factor (micrometers per pixel) ;; feature=Specific kinematic feature to compute (or NULL for all)
- alternatives: Fiji/ImageJ=Recommended for image registration and rotation to reduce unwanted specimen movements before importing into flowcatchR ;; External particle detectors=Users can import particle coordinates from other software using read.particles if they prefer not to use flowcatchR's segmentation
- when_to_use: Appropriate for analyzing time-lapse intravital microscopy images of flowing, rolling, or permanently adherent cells (such as platelets or leukocytes) in blood vessels to study phenomena like hemostasis and thrombosis development.
- pitfalls: Unregistered images=Living specimen movements can be confounded with true particle movements; images should be registered (e.g., via Fiji) beforehand ;; Spurious detections=Trajectories with 3 or less points will raise warnings in kinematics and will not have features computed ;; Flow direction assumptions=The tracking algorithm penalizes backward/perpendicular movements, so images should be rotated (e.g., via rotate.Frames) so the overall flow is oriented from left to right

workflows.name: cell_tracking_and_kinematics
workflows.intent: Track flowing blood cells in time-lapse microscopy images and analyze their kinematic properties.
input: image.files (a folder containing TIFF/JPG/PNG time-lapse microscopy images or a vector of image file paths)
workflows.stages:
1. Load raw images into a Frames object using read.Frames.
2. Extract the channel of interest (e.g., red for platelets) using channel.Frames.
3. Preprocess and segment the frames using preprocess.Frames.
4. Detect particles and extract features using particles.
5. Filter out noise particles based on area using select.particles.
6. Link particles across frames to form trajectories using link.particles.
7. Extract trajectories into a TrajectorySet using trajectories.
8. Calculate kinematic features (e.g., velocities, distances) using kinematics.
workflows.code:
library("flowcatchR")
data("MesenteriumSubset")

plateletsMesenterium <- channel.Frames(MesenteriumSubset, mode="red")

preprocessedPlatelets <- preprocess.Frames(plateletsMesenterium,
                                    brush.size=3, brush.shape="disc",
                                    at.offset=0.15, at.wwidth=10, at.wheight=10,
                                    kern.size=3, kern.shape="disc",
                                    ws.tolerance=1, ws.radius=1)

platelets <- particles(plateletsMesenterium, preprocessedPlatelets)

selectedPlatelets <- select.particles(platelets, min.area=3)

linkedPlatelets <- link.particles(platelets,  
                                  L=26, R=3,
                                  epsilon1=0, epsilon2=0,
                                  lambda1=1, lambda2=0,
                                  penaltyFunction=penaltyFunctionGenerator(),
                                  include.area=FALSE)

trajPlatelets <- trajectories(linkedPlatelets)

allKinematicFeats.allPlatelets <- kinematics(trajPlatelets,
                                             trajectoryIDs=NULL, # will select all trajectory IDs 
                                             acquisitionFrequency=30, # value in milliseconds
                                             scala=50, # 1 pixel is equivalent to ... micrometer
                                             feature=NULL) # all kinematic features available
